summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework set out in the country's own record. Provincially, gender identity and gender expression have been prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms since 2016, reaching employment, housing and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement is documented. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on the ground of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

Quebec's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial heard with 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021 QCCS 191). The Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement is the sharpest adverse finding in the provincial record. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province would be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety. The directive was issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz, convicted of murdering her partner and children, sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. The directive reverses the province's previous practice of considering gender identity in placement, and it bears on a visitor only if detained in Quebec.

On relationship recognition, Quebec created civil unions in 2002 by amending the Civil Code, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in matters of family, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance. That status is valid only in Quebec.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada's release of 30 March 2026 on police-reported hate crime for 2024 records 4,882 incidents nationally, a 1% rise on 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000 — down 2% over the year but up 142% since 2018. Provincial rates run from 5.3 per 100,000 in Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador to 16.0 in Ontario, with eight provinces stable or declining. The release carries no Quebec-specific rate figure, and its provincial comparison is by rate rather than by any trans-specific measure.

The underlying analysis of that police data used here is Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, produced by an LGBTIQ+ organisation and covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations. The national dataset itself breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity.

Widely cited national rankings of Canada's standing are framed around gay-friendliness and sexuality rather than transgender conditions specifically: first (least dangerous) in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 87.6% would be comfortable having a transgender neighbour, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour.

Montreal maintains a Gay Village and Pride is celebrated each summer in Quebec's major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political participation, which speaks to public visibility rather than to legal exposure.
localsOnly:
Quebec residents can bring discrimination complaints on the ground of gender identity or expression to the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal, and the tribunal's 10 June 2024 hiring decision shows the remedy available: moral and punitive damages plus arrears, awarded against a Montreal employer.

2021 census data cited by Éducaloi puts 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34, in the transgender population.

The civil union created by the 2002 Civil Code amendment is a Quebec-only status, conferring the effects of marriage within the province without being portable as a matter of provincial law.

The June 2025 correctional-placement directive applies to people held in Quebec institutions, and its stated basis of anatomical sex rather than gender identity governs where a transgender inmate is housed in the province.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Quebec-specific hate-crime rate appears in the Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026, and the release does not break out gender identity as a motivation. Trans-specific hate-crime volume in Quebec is therefore unresolved on these sources; the national and provincial figures cited are sexual-orientation-inclusive totals.

Whether the 19 June 2025 correctional-placement directive has been challenged in court, and whether it remains in force, is not sourced here. Advocates' assertion that it violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms is reported, not adjudicated, in the available material.

The provenance of the hate-crime analysis is an LGBTIQ+ organisation's report built on police-reported data, so under-reporting and police classification practices are not addressed by these sources.

National items — Criminal Code amendments, federal identity documents, other provinces' education and sport legislation, and the national human-rights and hate-motivation provisions — belong to the country record and are not restated here.
